extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientists concerned with conceptual clarity and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for forming, naming, and defining general conceptions used in inductive reasoning; guidance on how to choose, fix, and revise definitions so they serve scientific inquiry. Emphasizes appropriateness, clarity, observational grounding, and conformity with existing usage where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of a conception
rubrics_metrics.description: The conception must be appropriate — it should correspond to a real agreement among the phenomena and be suited to the particular object or purpose in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriateness is relative to purpose: a conception may be legitimately formed (e.g., grouping animals by color) but be inappropriate for certain investigations (e.g., studying structure or habits). Example: classing animals by skeleton structure is far more 'appropriate' for understanding anatomy than classing by color. Inappropriate conceptions miss important points of agreement or include irrelevant ones (Aristotle's 'toward its own place' conception of natural motion is given as an example of an inappropriate classificatory principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness (determinate conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions must be 'clear' — we must know exactly in what the agreement consists; the conception should be determinate, fixed, and not fluctuating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear conception requires careful observation, extensive experience, and accurate memory. It is sufficient that one always knows why items are classed together and never class things without knowing the specific common properties. A clear idea is one whose connotation (the properties it implies) is well ascertained and consistently applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception must correspond to a real agreement (applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the conception corresponds to a real agreement among the phenomena, it is inapplicable and therefore defective beyond mere vagueness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no real agreement exists among the instances to which a conception is applied, the conception cannot serve as a basis for induction. This is a separate defect from vagueness: a conception can be precise but still irrelevant if it does not pick out a genuine class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes must be real (real distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming classes we must ensure they are 'really a class' — the things included truly agree in certain particulars and differ in those same particulars from all other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person without clear ideas habitually groups things that have no common properties or properties shared widely by other things. Real classes are a prerequisite for asserting general truths applicable to those classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer properties important to your purpose (depth and relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When framing conceptions or classes, select the properties which go deepest into the nature of the things or are most closely connected with the particular property under investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all common properties are equally useful: choose those properties that are of primary importance for the theoretical or practical problem at hand — e.g., structure over color when studying organismal function. This improves 'appropriateness' for the specified purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature, dogmatic generalizations ('notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ')
rubrics_metrics.description: General conceptions formed without thorough knowledge often impede progress if they are permanently acquiesced in; premature abstractions must be open to revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making tentative general conceptions is inevitable in inquiry, but they are harmful only when treated as final. Habitual reliance on wrongly made classes (either unclear or inappropriate) blocks correction and progress; definitions should be revised as knowledge advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate observational and comparative habits
rubrics_metrics.description: The clearness and appropriateness of conceptions chiefly depend on careful observation and comparison; the activity of these faculties increases the chance of discovering the important agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A readiness in accurate observing and comparing leads one to perceive more and more quickly the agreements on which important consequences depend. Thus, habits of attentive observation, extensive experience, and good memory are principal requisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hypotheses and scientific imagination when mere comparison fails
rubrics_metrics.description: When important agreements are not discoverable by direct comparison of the phenomena, bring in previously acquired conceptions or hypotheses and exercise the scientific imagination to propose candidate generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The search for the common attribute can require conjecturing possible places or resemblances (like searching for a lost object). Such hypotheses should then be tested against the facts; prior conceptions and stored knowledge enable fruitful conjectures (example: planetary orbits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming (general names) as an instrument for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: General names and language are essential instruments for carrying induction beyond trivial particular-to-particular inference: they serve as an artificial memory and a way to record uniformities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without signs (words) we could only reason in very simple cases; general names allow us to remember and communicate uniformities discovered by experimentation and comparison. General names function as permanent signs of uniformities and make it practical to apply previously ascertained general truths to new cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every general name must have a meaning steadily fixed and precisely determined
rubrics_metrics.description: To be fit for the purposes of investigation and expression of general truths, every general name should have a certain and knowable meaning — its connotation must be fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general connotative name's meaning resides in the attributes it connotes; defining a name is fixing its connotation. Vagueness in common names (e.g., 'civilized', 'honor') undermines the ability to test general propositions by induction. Fixing connotation involves analyzing the marks by which the class is currently recognized and making those precise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide names where they are needed
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosophical or scientific language should supply a name wherever there is something important to express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming new distinctions or attributes is part of enabling clear thought and communication; lack of a term should not be a barrier to expressing or testing generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When defining existing names, conform to received use where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Fix the connotation of a term in a way that, as far as practicable, agrees with its current usages and the generally received propositions in which it appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is undesirable to force a meaning that conflicts with long-established associations or would render commonly accepted propositions false. The aim is to make the fixed connotation consistent with familiar usage so as to preserve existing true propositions while reducing vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition must be grounded in analysis of common attributes and selection of the most informative marks
rubrics_metrics.description: To define a concrete name you must compare the objects denoted and ascertain their common attributes, then select among these those which are the best marks (or causes) of other attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choice of attributes for a definition is not arbitrary: prefer attributes known by experience or deduction to be the basis of many other properties, or at least sure marks of them. Good definitions often require inductive work to discover unobvious agreements that explain obvious ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and connotations should progress with advancing knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to frame perfect definitions until the theory of the subject is perfect; as science progresses, definitions should be improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every enlargement of our knowledge of the objects to which a name is applied may suggest an improved definition. Definitions are therefore tentative and subject to refinement as underlying theory becomes more complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explication of conceptions (unfolding definitions) is a logical task
rubrics_metrics.description: Explication consists in ascertaining in what particulars phenomena classed together really agree — making the connotation of a name explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many scientific controversies take the form of disputes over definitions; such disputes acquire value because there is an associated substantive proposition or theory that the definition is intended to express. The logician's task is to analyze vague common impressions into precise attributes that constitute the class.
